planting.note: Root stem segments in a loose, fast-draining orchid-bark cactus mix in bright indirect light to light shade; this epiphyte forms interlocking triangular stem links rather than typical cactus pads.

directions: Grow in a loose, well-aerated orchid-bark cactus mix in bright, indirect light or dappled shade, keeping the roots lightly moist during active growth and drier in winter. Rhipsalis paradoxa is native to the humid forests of Brazil and Argentina and is instantly recognizable by its three-angled stem segments that twist and link together like the loops of a coarse chain, an unusual branching habit distinct from the thinner, rounder stems of its Rhipsalis relatives. Small pale flowers appear at the segment joints in winter, occasionally followed by translucent berries. Because it grows naturally lodged in tree bark and leaf litter rather than soil, it prefers a chunky, quick-draining medium and steady humidity over rich potting soil, and its cascading, sculptural stems are best displayed in a hanging basket where the distinctive chain-link segments can dangle freely.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Root callused stem cuttings in a loose orchid-bark cactus mix in bright indirect light or light shade; the fine hairs covering the stems and fruit trap humidity and should not be misted heavily to avoid rot.

directions: Grow in a loose, well-drained orchid-bark cactus mix in bright indirect light to light shade, watering when the top layer of mix dries but never letting the roots sit wet. Native to the coastal forests of Brazil, Rhipsalis pilocarpa is a distinctive jungle cactus whose cylindrical stems and later its round berries are covered in fine, soft white hairs, giving the whole plant a fuzzy, almost velvety texture unlike the smooth stems of most Rhipsalis species. Cream-white flowers appear along the stems in winter and are followed by pink-tinged, hairy fruit that persist for weeks, adding ornamental interest beyond the trailing foliage. As an epiphyte adapted to filtered canopy light and humid but airy conditions, it resents heavy, waterlogged soil and stagnant air, so provide good air circulation alongside consistent but moderate moisture.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery stock in spring in well-drained, gritty succulent mix in bright indirect light to partial sun; grow only as a hanging basket or shelf plant, since it has essentially no cold tolerance.

directions: This selection of string of hearts carries broader, more rounded leaves with heavier, more even silver marbling than the standard species, giving the trailing stems a cooler, almost pewter-toned look rather than the pink-flushed variegation of 'Variegata'. Because the leaves retain more chlorophyll than variegated forms, 'Silver Glory' tends to grow a bit more vigorously and tolerates slightly lower light than heavily variegated string of hearts cultivars, though it still colors best with a few hours of bright, indirect light or gentle morning sun. Let the gritty, fast-draining mix dry out completely between waterings, since the tuberous stems and aerial bead-like tubers are prone to rot in consistently damp soil. Propagate by rooting stem cuttings with at least one node in spring or summer to fill out a hanging basket or start new plants.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Plant Selector (Ceropegia woodii)
North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox — Ceropegia

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant on a small trellis or in a hanging basket in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix; this twining vine stores water in succulent stems and a tuberous base and prefers to dry out between waterings.

directions: Grow as a houseplant on a small trellis or in a hanging basket in bright, indirect light in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix, allowing the medium to dry fully between waterings. Native to South Africa, Ceropegia ampliata is a twining succulent vine that sheds its few narrow juvenile leaves as it matures, leaving smooth, jointed green stems that climb or trail by twisting around any available support. In summer it produces striking, waxy, white-and-green striped flowers shaped like small hanging lanterns, fused at the tip into a cage that temporarily traps small fly pollinators before releasing them dusted in pollen, much like its relative the parachute plant. Provide a small support for the twining stems to climb, and grow from a semi-tuberous base that stores water through dry spells, making it forgiving of occasional missed waterings.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Mount on a slab or grow in a hanging basket in bright, indirect light in a loose, fast-draining, orchid-bark-based epiphytic mix; ant plant is a true epiphyte and rots quickly in dense, moisture-retentive potting soil.

directions: Mount on cork bark or a fern slab, or grow loosely potted in a hanging basket, in bright, indirect light within a chunky, fast-draining orchid-bark mix, watering only once the medium has dried. Native to the Philippines, Dischidia pectinoides is grown chiefly for its curious swollen, hollow leaf pouches, which in the wild are colonized by ants that bring in debris and nutrients while the plant absorbs moisture and minerals through roots growing inside the cavity, making it one of the more striking myrmecophytic, or ant-associated, houseplants. Alongside the inflated pouches, thinner, flatter succulent leaves are borne on wiry trailing stems, and small orange-red tubular flowers appear sporadically. Provide bright filtered light, high humidity, and excellent air movement, and avoid burying the pouches in potting mix, since they function best exposed to air just as they would on a rainforest tree branch.
sources: American Orchid Society — epiphyte cultivation reference
